claims.text: Available analytical predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr have limited accuracy and rely on perfect, defect-free crystals.
A defect-sensitive machine-learning regression model will predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical models.
The proposed regression model will be trained using a combined dataset of ab initio defect-scattering simulations and experimental conductivity measurements.
Quantum and impurity scattering effects dominate electrical behavior in the 0–200 K regime.
Phonon scattering and defect dynamics are significant in the 300–1200 K regime.
Conductivity measurements are available for bulk HfNbTaTiZr in the stated cryogenic and high-temperature regimes, including for material containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Effective defect density and oxygen impurity concentration will be explicit model features.
Lattice defects and oxygen impurities introduce carrier-scattering mechanisms that affect the alloy's electrical conductivity.
Encoding defect density and oxygen concentration will allow predictions to reflect the actual microstructural state of the alloy.
Accounting for the real microstructural state will overcome systematic errors caused by perfect-crystal assumptions.
The model's conductivity predictions will closely track measurements throughout both 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The model will have smaller conductivity-prediction errors than perfect-crystal analytical models.
Perfect-crystal analytical predictions will systematically deviate from observations, especially for oxygen-contaminated samples.
The proposed model is intended to apply only within 0–200 K and 300–1200 K and to samples containing no more than 1 wt.% oxygen.
Model performance may deteriorate when defect densities or impurity levels fall outside the training-data parameter space.
The magnitude of improvement depends on the quality, representativeness, and extent of the defect and impurity information in the training dataset.
Unrepresented defect types, oxygen effects, or other scattering mechanisms could reduce model accuracy.

The hypothesis will be falsified if the model fails to achieve a statistically significant error reduction in both temperature regimes or fails to capture the conductivity trend caused by 1 wt.% oxygen.
